title: Exception Handling
description: Handling runtime errors gracefully with try/except/else/finally, raising exceptions, and custom exception classes.
objectives: Distinguish syntax errors, runtime errors, and logical errors
Raise exceptions and define custom exception classes

content.heading: Kinds of Errors and try/except
content.body:
It's useful to distinguish three kinds of problems: syntax errors (the code isn't even valid Python — caught before the program runs), runtime errors / exceptions (the code is valid but something goes wrong while executing, like dividing by zero or accessing a missing dictionary key), and logical errors (the code runs without crashing but produces the wrong result — these are the hardest to catch automatically, since nothing 'fails').

A try block wraps code that might raise an exception; one or more except clauses catch specific exception types and handle them. Catching the most specific exception type you expect (except ZeroDivisionError:) is much better practice than a bare except: or except Exception:, which can silently swallow bugs you didn't anticipate. An optional else clause runs only if the try block completed with no exception. A finally clause always runs, whether or not an exception occurred — ideal for cleanup code (closing a file or connection) that must happen regardless of outcome.

content.heading: Raising Exceptions and Custom Exception Classes
content.body: raise ValueError("message") explicitly triggers an exception, useful for validating function inputs. Python's built-in exceptions form a hierarchy rooted at BaseException (with Exception as the ancestor of most 'normal' errors you should catch); catching a parent class also catches all its subclasses, so except Exception: catches nearly everything. You can define your own exception types by subclassing Exception (or a more specific built-in exception), which lets calling code catch your specific error condition separately from unrelated ones. except (TypeError, ValueError) as e: catches multiple exception types in one clause. Exception chaining (raise NewError(...) from original_error) preserves the original traceback when translating one exception into another, which is valuable for debugging.

keyPoints: Syntax errors are caught before running; runtime errors (exceptions) happen during execution; logical errors produce wrong results silently
Catch the most specific exception type you can — avoid bare except:
else runs only on success; finally always runs, ideal for cleanup
Custom exception classes (subclassing Exception) let callers handle specific failure conditions distinctly
commonMistakes: Using a bare except: (or except Exception: pass) that silently hides real bugs
Forgetting that finally runs even when a return or another exception happens inside the try/except
Raising a generic Exception instead of a specific or custom exception type, making it hard for callers to react precisely
